Visible chromosome gaps, breaks, and structural rearrangements are found in blood lym- phocytes from patients who have received substantial doses of combination chemotherapy, and the changes persist for years after the end of treatment. A more sensitive, if transient, measure of genetic damage is the increased rate of sister chro- matid exchange (SCE) that occurs with even quite small dos- es of cytotoxic drugs.1 Evidence from a study2 in patients giv- en chlorambucil suggests that as the dose increases so the capacity of the cells to cope with induced genetic damage is progressively exceeded, and thus SCE frequency reflects cu- mulative toxicity throughout the course of treatment.
